parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones an airport car park company to book parking for a family holiday.
script: Good afternoon, Skyline Airport Parking, Sandra speaking. How can I help?
Hello. I'd like to book parking for about a week in August, please. We're flying out of Eastmoor Airport.
Certainly. I'll just take a few details first. Can I have your name?
And could you spell your surname for me?
H-A-R-G-R-E-A-V-E-S. Thank you. And a contact number, in case we need to reach you about the booking?
07702 483 916. Lovely. And where are you flying to, Mr Hargreaves? I like to check, because we get a lot of flight changes at this time of year.
Lisbon. We're staying there for a couple of days and then travelling up to Porto by train, but the flight itself is to Lisbon.
Lisbon, fine. And what date do you leave?
On 13 August. Oh, sorry, no, hang on. I was looking at the hotel booking. The flight is on 12 August.
12 August. And when do you come back?
On the 20th. The flight was due to land at 20.15, but the airline emailed last week to say it's been retimed, so it's now 20.45.
20.45 on 20 August, so that's eight days in all. Good, that's the time I need, so we know when to expect you. Now, what car will you be leaving with us?
It's a Skoda, an estate, dark green. My wife has a little Fiat as well, but we'll be taking the Skoda because of the luggage.

Right, a Skoda. Now, we have three options. The Saver car park is the cheapest, but it's about 2 miles from the terminal, with a shuttle bus every half hour. The Express car park is only five minutes away, with a bus every ten minutes. And the Premium car park is a short walk from the terminal.
The Saver is 6 pounds a day, the Express is 10 pounds 50, and the Premium is 16 pounds.
Hmm. I was going to go for the Saver, but a bus only every half hour when we land late, with two tired children? I think we'd better take the Express.
That's what most families choose. So that's eight days at 10 pounds 50 a day, which comes to 84 pounds.
That's fine. Is it all right to pay when I arrive?

No, I'm afraid you pay now, by card, and I'll take the details in a moment. Would you like any extras? A lot of our customers pay for a car wash while they're away. It's 12 pounds. We also do a fuel top-up, or an oil check.

A fuel top-up would be useful, but I'd rather fill the tank myself. The car wash is a good idea, though. There's building work near our house and the car is covered in dust. Yes, please add the car wash.

No problem. Now, on the day, you'll go to Orchard Car Park. Please don't follow the signs for Terminal Parking, because that's the Premium one. The Saver customers go to Meadow, but you want Orchard. It's off the roundabout just after the petrol station.

That's right. When you park, hand your keys in at the cabin by the gate, and the shuttle will take you to the departures hall. Please aim to arrive at the car park at least three hours before your flight, because it can get busy.
Three hours, understood. And on the way back, what do I do?
When you land, just give us a ring from the baggage hall and the shuttle will meet you outside the arrivals door. It's usually there in about ten minutes.
Brilliant. Thank you very much for your help.
My pleasure. Now, can I take your card number?

groups.instr: Complete the form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
groups.heading: Skyline Airport Parking: booking form

items.why: The surname is spelled out letter by letter: H-A-R-G-R-E-A-V-E-S.
He gives his mobile number as 07702 483 916.
He travels on to Porto by train, but the flight itself is to Lisbon.
He first says 13 August, then corrects himself: the flight is on 12 August (13 was the hotel booking).
The original time was 20.15, but the airline has retimed the flight to 20.45.
They take the Skoda, not his wife's Fiat.
He considers the Saver but rejects it because of the half-hourly bus; he chooses the Express.
Eight days at 10 pounds 50 a day is 84 pounds. The car wash (12 pounds) is an extra and is not included.
He declines to pay for a fuel top-up because he will fill the tank himself, and chooses the car wash.
Orchard is the car park for the Express service; Meadow is for Saver and Terminal Parking is Premium.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A guide gives an introduction at the start of a tasting tour of a city food market.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Saltgate Market Tasting Tour. My name's Marama, and I'll be your guide for the morning. Before we set off, I'd like to give you a little background and run through a few practical points.

Saltgate Market has stood on this site since 1887, when it was a small fish market beside the old harbour. Today there are more than 150 stalls under one roof, and about 8000 people shop here on a busy Saturday. The tour was started six years ago by a group of traders who thought visitors were missing the best of the market because they didn't know where to look.

First, the meeting point. Some of you went to the information kiosk in Hall 1 this morning, which is a very natural thing to do, and it's where we used to start. Our old leaflets also mention the clock tower, because that's what the tour was called years ago. But since last spring we've started every tour at the Hall 2 entrance, which is where you found me. If you recommend us to friends, please tell them that, because the odd person still ends up waiting at the wrong place.

Now, how long will it take? The brochure still says two hours, and that was true until recently. But this year we've added a ninth stop, so you should allow two and a half hours altogether. You'll have plenty of time to ask questions, and nobody will rush you.

A word about what to wear. The fish hall is washed down every morning, and the floor can be wet, so I'd recommend flat shoes with a good grip. There's no need to bring a coat, because the halls are heated throughout the winter. As for bags, you're welcome to buy things as we go, and every stallholder has paper bags, so there's no need to carry anything.

Next, the tasting itself. You'll try something at every stop, but the portions are quite small. It's best to have only a light breakfast beforehand. Please tell me now if you have any allergies or dislikes, because I can arrange substitutes with the stallholders.

Something that's new this year is a vegetarian route. If you don't eat meat or fish, you can now book a version of the tour that skips the fish hall and the sausage stall, and visits two extra stalls instead. We did think about a mobile phone app, and a souvenir tote bag as well, but those will have to wait until next year, because we ran out of budget.

Right, a quick preview of what's coming. Our first stop is Pemberton's Bakery. It's been in the same family for three generations, and what makes it special is that the flour comes from the owner's own farm, 30 miles north of the city. You can taste the difference, I promise.

Next, we walk across to Old Mill Cheese. Their stall is small and rather easy to miss, but last year they were named the city's best food producer, and the certificate is in the window. They'll let you sample three cheeses, and I'd suggest the smoked one.

After that we move into the fish hall, to Ocean Pier. This is the oldest stall in the market. The family have traded from the very same spot since the first day in 1887, and the current owner still keeps the original brass scales on the counter. You may not fancy raw fish at this time in the morning, but the smoked salmon is excellent.

From there we cross the main aisle to Gaia Spices. They only moved into their present position in March. For years they were in the old arcade at the back, and a lot of regular customers didn't realise they'd gone. Do say hello to the owner, Mrs Dhillon, who will explain what all those jars contain.

Then comes one of my favourites, Tanaka's Noodles. Many of our stalls only open at weekends, but Tanaka's is open six days a week, and the best thing is that you stand at the counter and watch the noodles being pulled and cut by hand in front of you. People take photographs, so have your phones ready.

Finally, we finish at Hartley Chocolates. Everything they sell is dairy-free, and there's nothing made from animal products at all, which surprises people, because the chocolate tastes so rich. It's a lovely place to end, and there's a bench where you can sit down.

So, that's the plan. One last thing: if you'd like to keep in touch, there's a sign-up sheet at the last stop, and we'll send you our seasonal recipes. Now, if everyone is ready, please follow me, and we'll make our way to the bakery.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Chloe and Aiden, plan a science fair demonstration on solar ovens.
script: Hi, Aiden. Have you got a minute? I wanted to go through the solar oven demonstration before we meet Dr Patel on Thursday.
Sure. I've just been reading her comments on our proposal, actually.
Oh, what did she say? I only skimmed it.

Well, she liked the idea, which is a relief. She was a bit worried that it might be too ambitious, but then she saw we're only building one oven, so that was fine. The main thing was that we hadn't said clearly what we want visitors to understand when they leave our stall.
Right, a clearer aim. So something like, sunlight can cook food if you trap the heat.
Exactly. And she checked, there's no other group doing solar cooking, so we don't overlap with anyone.
Good. Now, the oven itself. I looked into three designs. There's the pizza box one, the plastic bucket one, and the wooden crate one.
I do like the bucket, because it's so cheap, but it's tricky to line properly, isn't it? All those curves.
That's what I thought. And the crate would be far too heavy to carry on the train. So I think it has to be the pizza box.
Fine by me. I can get hold of some boxes from the pizzeria near my flat.

Great. I made a trial one last weekend, with foil on the inside of the flap and black paper on the bottom. It only reached about 60 degrees, and I was convinced it was because it was cloudy, or because the foil was crinkled and wasn't reflecting properly.
Neither, as it turned out. I held my hand along the edges and I could feel warm air leaking out through the gaps where the lid meets the box. Once I sealed it with tape, it went up to 85.
That's a big difference. So we need to make sure the lid fits tightly. I'll add that to the notes.
Now, what should we actually cook? Dr Patel suggested eggs, but I think they take too long.
And there's the food hygiene issue, isn't there? Raw eggs at a public event, no thanks.
Exactly. What about toast? No, that would be slow as well. Marshmallows start to melt at quite a low temperature, so they'd work fast, and visitors love them.
Marshmallows it is, then. Simple, quick, and everybody can see them change.
The other problem is that the fair is indoors, in the sports hall, so there won't be any sun. I wondered whether we could film the oven working outside and play the video on a screen.
I'm not sure. People will want to see it happen live. Dr Patel said they allow lamps, so I could borrow a halogen lamp from the physics lab. It's 500 watts, which should be enough.
Yes, you're right. A lamp is better than a video. Let's do that.
Okay. So let's plan the actual demonstration. I think we should make a poster first.
Yes. I was going to put in lots of photos of us building the oven.
Hmm, photos are nice, but I think visitors will learn more from a large diagram that shows how the foil reflects the light into the box. We can add one or two photos around the edge.
A diagram, you're right. I'll draw that. Next, the oven itself. It will get hot underneath, so we can't put it straight on the table.
I've got some spare ceramic tile from my bathroom project. We can stand the oven on a tile.
Perfect. Then we need something to prop the lid open at the right angle so that it catches the light. I was going to use a wooden spoon.
A ruler would be better. It's rigid, and we can mark the angle on it so that it's the same every time.
Good idea. How long do the marshmallows need? Outside, it takes about 10 minutes, I think.
Yes, but under a lamp the light is weaker, so we should allow 20 minutes. That's fine, we can talk to visitors while we wait.
Right, 20 minutes. And finally, we should give visitors something to take away. I thought about a booklet, with instructions on how to build their own oven.
A booklet would cost too much to print for a whole day. A single-page leaflet is enough, with the steps and a list of materials.
A leaflet, then. I'll design it tonight. Let's go and see Dr Patel.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about the economics of second-hand clothing.
script: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to look at an industry that most of us take part in without ever thinking about it: the global trade in second-hand clothing. When you drop a bag of unwanted jumpers at a charity shop, you probably imagine them hanging on a rail down the road a week later. For most of those garments, the reality is very different, and the economics behind it are surprisingly complex.

Let me begin with the supply side. Over the last twenty years, clothing has become so cheap in wealthy countries that we treat it as almost disposable. Industry researchers estimate that the average garment is now worn only 7 times before it is thrown away or given away. In the year 2000, the figure was around 14. In other words, cheap, fast-changing fashion has doubled the speed at which our wardrobes turn over, and every one of those discarded items has to go somewhere.

Charity shops are the most visible destination, but they are not the main one. They receive far more than they can sell: only about 20 per cent of donated clothing is ever bought in the shop it was given to. A generation ago, the figure was closer to a third. The rest is sold on to commercial sorting companies, who pay by weight, and this is where the international trade begins.

In a large sorting warehouse, workers stand at conveyor belts and grade items by hand. They are remarkably quick, deciding in a couple of seconds whether a coat is fit for resale in a boutique, for a market stall abroad, or only for recycling as rags. There may be as many as 300 categories, based on fabric, brand, condition and season. The very best garments, perhaps four or five per cent of the total, are known in the trade as cream.

Everything else is pressed into bales. A standard bale weighs 55 kilograms, although some exporters prefer smaller ones of 45 for shipping reasons. A bale is then sold to a wholesaler, usually in Asia, Eastern Europe or Africa, and here is a point that surprises many students. Buyers generally don't open the bales before they pay. They rely on the grade label and the reputation of the supplier, but the contents are never certain. Many traders describe buying a bale as something of a lottery: some contain a dozen high-value jackets, while others hold almost nothing that can be sold.

Let's turn to the effects on the importing countries. For many people on low incomes, second-hand clothing is the only affordable way to dress well, and the trade also supports a huge number of jobs: importers, porters, washers, market traders and so on. In some East African cities, the second-hand markets are among the largest employers in the informal economy.

However, there is a downside. As imports increased, local clothing factories found it very hard to compete, and in several countries the domestic textile industry shrank dramatically. In response, a few governments have tried to ban imports in order to protect local manufacturers, though the results have been mixed. Bans have led to smuggling, higher prices and, in at least one case, trade penalties imposed by a larger economy.

Before we condemn the whole trade, though, consider the creativity within it. Many traders employ tailors to alter garments, taking in a coat, shortening a pair of trousers, or even turning one item into something completely different. These small businesses add value in a way that factory clothing does not. They also lengthen the life of the garment, which brings me to the environmental side of the argument.

Producing a single cotton shirt takes around 2700 litres of water, according to one widely used estimate. That is roughly what a person drinks over two and a half years. Every extra year of use spreads that cost over a longer period, so a thriving second-hand market is, in principle, good for the environment. The problem arises when garments are shipped thousands of miles, only to end up unsold on a rubbish tip.

So what are policy-makers doing about this? Several countries in Europe are moving towards systems of extended producer responsibility, in which fashion brands would pay a fee for every garment they sell, to cover the cost of collection and recycling. France introduced a version some years ago, and other countries are studying it closely.

Finally, researchers have recommended an improvement in labelling. At the moment, recyclers cannot easily tell what a garment is made of, and mixed fabrics are almost impossible to separate. If every item carried a clear label stating its fibre content, sorting would be faster, and far more clothing could be recycled instead of being thrown away.

passages.title: Mapping the Lost City
paras: A  For more than a century, explorers have told stories of a vanished city hidden beneath the forest canopy of the Tamoch lowlands. In 1894 the naturalist Hugo Brandt returned from a three-month expedition with sketches of a stepped pyramid, a few carved stones and a conviction that the ruins he had glimpsed were only the edge of something far larger. Nobody could prove him right. The forest there is so dense that a person standing ten metres from a stone wall may not see it, and ground survey is painfully slow: a team of four archaeologists, cutting paths with machetes, might map a single hectare in a fortnight. At that rate, surveying the 3,000 square kilometres in which the city was thought to lie would have taken several lifetimes.

B  The breakthrough came from the air. Lidar, short for light detection and ranging, works by firing rapid pulses of laser light from an aircraft towards the ground and timing how long each one takes to return. A modern instrument can send out 500,000 pulses every second. Most of them bounce off leaves and branches, but a small proportion slip through gaps in the canopy and reach the soil. Because the laser records every return separately, software can sort the pulses by height, discard those that struck vegetation and use the remainder to build a "bare-earth" model of the terrain. The effect is like stripping the forest away digitally, leaving a detailed relief map in which even a wall half a metre high casts a visible shadow.

C  In 2019 a consortium led by Dr Elena Marchetti flew lidar across 1,200 square kilometres of the Tamoch lowlands in just eleven days. When the first images appeared on her screen, she later recalled, she assumed there had been an error. Until then the site of Kolhun, as the city had come to be called, was believed to be a ceremonial centre of about five square kilometres, housing perhaps 10,000 people. The survey revealed an urban landscape covering nearly 90 square kilometres, with some 38,000 structures: house platforms, terraces, causeways, plazas and ball courts. Revised population estimates now range from 80,000 to well over 100,000, making Kolhun comparable in size to the largest cities in Europe at the same period.

D  Images alone, however, do not amount to archaeology. A lidar map shows shapes, not dates or purposes, and the team knew that a good many of the features it highlighted might be natural or recent. The next phase, known as ground-truthing, therefore involved small parties walking to a sample of locations with GPS units to confirm what lay there. One apparent "fortification" proved to be a field boundary built by farmers in the 1950s, and around one in eight of the sites visited turned out to be a misreading of natural ridges. Dr Marchetti insists that these errors strengthen rather than weaken the method. "Every wrong guess teaches the software, and the people interpreting it, something," she says. Dating still depends on traditional techniques: excavation, pottery analysis and radiocarbon testing of charcoal found in sealed layers.

E  The survey's most important finding may concern water. Running across the map are networks of reservoirs joined by channels, some more than 12 kilometres long, which fed fields laid out on terraced slopes. Such works imply central planning and sophisticated engineering, and they challenge an old theory that the thin soils of tropical forests could never have supported large permanent cities. Instead, the farmers of Kolhun appear to have managed their land intensively for at least six centuries, abandoning it only after a series of long droughts. Archaeologists now suspect that similar cities lie undiscovered elsewhere in the region.

F  Lidar is not a miracle cure. Hiring an aircraft and instrument costs the equivalent of several hundred pounds per square kilometre, which puts large surveys beyond most university departments, and a single flight generates terabytes of data that take months to process. The technique also reveals nothing about anything buried deeper than the surface, such as tombs. A more troubling consequence is that maps showing exactly where ancient structures stand are also maps for looters. After the first results were published, illegal digging was reported at three sites, and the government has since insisted that precise coordinates should be withheld from public reports.

G  The next generation of research is likely to combine lidar with drone-mounted sensors and machine-learning software capable of recognising the patterns of buried buildings automatically. Yet Dr Marchetti argues that the most valuable resource may be human rather than technical. Villagers living in the lowlands had known about many of the mounds for generations, and several local guides were able to name terraces that the team had labelled only with numbers. Her team now employs members of the local community as co-researchers, and she believes the future of the field depends on treating those who live beside such sites not as bystanders but as partners.

passages.title: The Secrets of Long Lives
paras: A  Few questions in biology are as stubborn as why some animals live so much longer than others. A house mouse is old at two; a human may reach ninety; but the record-holders are found in the sea. In 2016 an international team announced that the Greenland shark, a slow, pale predator of the Arctic deep, can live for at least 250 years, making it the longest-lived vertebrate known. Because sharks have no bones or growth rings, the researchers estimated ages by measuring radiocarbon in the lens of the eye, a tissue that forms before birth and is never replaced. Bowhead whales are nearly as impressive: stone harpoon tips lodged in the blubber of living animals show that some individuals have survived for more than two centuries. For biologists, such creatures are living experiments in how ageing might be delayed.

B  Size alone cannot explain such longevity, although large animals do tend, on average, to outlive small ones. The puzzle is that a whale's body contains thousands of times more cells than a human's, and every cell division carries a small risk of a cancerous mutation. In theory, whales and elephants should therefore die of cancer far more often than people do; in practice they rarely do. This apparent contradiction is known as Peto's paradox, after the epidemiologist who first drew attention to it. Part of the answer seems to lie in genes. Elephants possess around twenty copies of a gene that triggers the self-destruction of damaged cells, whereas humans have only one. Bowhead whales, by contrast, appear to owe their resistance to unusually efficient genes for DNA repair, which allow them to mend breaks in their genetic material before they become dangerous.

C  The naked mole-rat shows that the strategy need not depend on size at all. This hairless rodent, no bigger than a mouse, lives for more than thirty years in underground colonies in East Africa, and it almost never develops tumours. Its cells produce an unusually thick, sugar-based substance called hyaluronan, which prevents them from crowding together; crowded cells are more likely to take one of the early steps towards a tumour. Stranger still, the mole-rat's chance of dying does not rise as it grows older, which breaks a rule that holds for nearly every other mammal studied. It can also survive for long periods on very little oxygen, a skill that perhaps evolved in the stale air of its burrows. Researchers who study these animals describe them as the closest thing yet found to a creature that does not age in the usual way.

D  Bats offer a different lesson. The Brandt's bat weighs about seven grams, yet one individual in Siberia was recaptured after forty-one years, a record for a mammal of its size. Biologists believe the secret may lie in telomeres, the protective caps at the ends of chromosomes. Each time a cell divides, its telomeres become a little shorter, and when they are too short the cell stops dividing. This process is widely regarded as a molecular clock of ageing. In several bat species, however, telomeres do not shorten with age, probably because the animals have genes that rebuild them. Hibernation, which cuts the body's energy use for months at a time, may help as well, since a cell that works slowly has less opportunity to accumulate damage.

E  Hibernation points to an older idea, the "rate of living" theory, which proposed that every animal has a fixed quantity of energy to burn in a lifetime, so that those with fast metabolisms must die young. It explains the giant tortoise well: with a heart rate of only a few beats per minute and a metabolism to match, it can live for more than 150 years. But the theory has been badly damaged by birds. A pigeon's metabolism is far faster than a rat's, yet pigeons live for years longer. Most biologists now treat metabolic rate as only one factor among many, and regard the damaging by-products of energy production, such as free radicals, as something that animals can learn to control rather than an inescapable cost of being alive.

F  A broader explanation comes from evolution. Natural selection cares about survival only up to the point of reproduction, and animals that face a high risk of being eaten or starved gain little from investing in a body built to last. Where danger is low, however, the calculation changes. Bats can fly away; tortoises carry armour; mole-rats live in sealed tunnels; and bowhead whales are too large for most predators. A classic study compared opossums living on the mainland with those on a nearby island free of predators. The island animals matured later, bred more slowly and lived about 25 per cent longer, just as the theory predicts. Safe lives, in other words, appear to select for slow ageing.

G  Will these discoveries one day help people? Scientists are cautious. Experiments in which mice were engineered to produce mole-rat-style hyaluronan showed lower rates of cancer, but the benefits were modest, and what works in a short-lived rodent may not translate to a primate. Most researchers also point out that extending the human life span is not the real aim. The more realistic goal is to extend healthspan, the number of years lived free from serious illness, so that people spend less of their later lives in poor health. If the long-lived animals have a single lesson to teach, it is that ageing is not one process but many, and that each species has found its own ways of slowing it down.

passages.title: Should the Treasures Go Home?
paras: A  In the great hall of a national museum in a European capital, a bronze head gazes over the visitors towards a case of Roman coins. It was made by court craftsmen six hundred years ago in a kingdom that no longer exists, and it was carried to Europe in 1897 in the baggage of a soldier. It is one of tens of thousands of objects in Western museums whose origins lie elsewhere, and the question of what should become of them is among the most heated in the cultural world. I believe that the debate is too often presented as a choice between two absolutes, keep everything or return everything, and that both positions fail on their own terms.

B  The case for keeping objects where they are rests on what is usually called the "universal museum" argument: the idea that great museums are the common property of humanity, where objects from many cultures can be compared under one roof and seen by millions of visitors each year. Professor Tomas Lindqvist, a lawyer who advises several museum boards, adds a legal point: most acquisitions took place decades or centuries before modern conventions existed, and judging them by today's standards would be both unfair and, in practice, unworkable. There is something in this. But it is striking how rarely the universal museum is universal in the sense that matters. Its visitors are overwhelmingly those who can afford to travel to a handful of wealthy cities, and I find the notion that the people from whom an object was taken are somehow represented by its presence abroad unconvincing.

C  A second argument holds that source countries could not look after the objects if they were returned. This may have been true in the 1960s; it is much harder to defend now. Dr Amara Nwosu, who directs a new museum built to house returned artefacts, points out that her institution has climate-controlled galleries, a conservation laboratory and insurance comparable to those of any European museum. "The question of who is competent to care for these things," she says, "sounds a good deal more like prejudice than like science." I am inclined to agree with her. Nobody suggests that a collection should be moved because the museum that holds it is poorly run, and there is no reason to apply a stricter test to museums in the countries of origin than to those in Europe.

D  Yet the return-everything position has weaknesses of its own. Many objects were not stolen at all but bought, commissioned or given as gifts, and it would be as wrong to treat every collector as a looter as it would be to treat every one as a saint. Furthermore, the borders of today's states often bear little relation to the cultures that produced the objects. To whom, exactly, should a sculpture made in a vanished empire be returned: the state that now occupies its territory, or the community that claims descent from its makers? Where several claimants exist, a ruling in favour of one may generate a dispute rather than resolve one. These are practical problems, not excuses, and they cannot be solved by slogans.

E  Where, then, do I stand? My view is that there is a clear moral case for restitution when objects were taken by force, as in military campaigns, or by fraud, and when the provenance, the documented history of ownership, can be established. In these cases the passage of time does not alter what happened; it merely makes it more convenient to forget. A handful of museums have already begun to act on this principle by returning items looted in nineteenth-century wars, and in no case so far has the feared collapse of a collection followed. The fear that one return would open the floodgates has proved, so far, to be exaggerated.

F  For the large number of cases where the history is less clear, I think returning everything is neither necessary nor wise, and better solutions exist. Long-term loans, shared custody and joint exhibitions allow objects to move in both directions, and they allow experts from both sides to work together. Ms Kalinda Rei, a curator from a Pacific island nation, describes her museum's arrangement to display a carved canoe prow jointly with a London institution as "the first time we were asked rather than told". Digital copies, though often proposed as a compromise, strike me as a poor substitute: a three-dimensional scan can be admired, but it cannot be touched, honoured or, in some cases, used in the ceremonies for which the original was made.

G  There is also a danger that attention to restitution distracts from more pressing problems. Museums in poorer countries often struggle with leaking roofs and unpaid staff, and a returned masterpiece will not by itself solve that. If wealthy museums were to spend even a fraction of the sums they devote to acquisitions on helping partners build skills and facilities, the benefit would reach far more objects than the few that are in dispute. The debate will not end soon, but it would be better served by patience and open minds than by the dogmatic claims that have too often dominated it. The bronze head in the great hall has its own story to tell, and its future should be decided by those who know that story best.
